title: Reef Fish Dodge Black Disk at Near‑2 m/s as Bar Jacks Attack on Curaçao Reef—Space Daily
body:
A new underwater experiment off the coast of Curaçao has pinpointed the exact speed at which reef fish abandon a safe haven, revealing that a black, expanding disc projected from an iPad can trigger a flight response at just under two metres per second. The finding, which emerged from a series of high‑resolution video recordings on a coral patch, also documented that predatory bar jacks on the same reef can accelerate to between 2.7 and 9.0 m s⁻¹, comfortably exceeding the fish’s escape threshold. The research offers fresh insight into the visual cues that govern predator‑prey dynamics in complex reef ecosystems and could inform future conservation strategies that rely on behavioural manipulation.

The experiment was conducted on a shallow reef flat where a transparent acrylic platform held a tablet displaying a solid black circle that grew in size at a controlled rate. As the disc expanded, its apparent approach speed—calculated from the change in visual angle—was incrementally increased. Researchers observed the resident damselfish, cardinalfish and other small reef dwellers, noting the exact moment each individual broke off from the coral patch and fled. Below a projected speed of roughly 1.9 m s⁻¹, none of the fish displayed any alarm; they continued to forage and interact as normal. Once the disc’s expansion crossed that threshold, a cascade of rapid escapes unfolded, with fish darting into the water column or seeking refuge in crevices.

Parallel footage captured the hunting behaviour of the bar jack (Caranx ruber), a mid‑size predatory fish that frequents the same patch. Using a combination of underwater GoPro cameras and acoustic telemetry, the team measured the jacks’ burst speeds during pursuit sequences. The predators routinely reached speeds of 2.7 m s⁻¹ during the initial chase, with peak bursts climbing to 9.0 m s⁻¹ when closing in on fleeing prey. These figures place the bar jack’s acceleration well above the fish’s escape threshold, confirming that the predator’s approach is fast enough to overwhelm the visual cue‑based defence mechanisms of its targets.

The implications extend beyond a simple speed comparison. Visual perception on the reef is heavily influenced by “looming” – the rapid expansion of an object’s image on the retina, which signals imminent collision. The study’s controlled looming stimulus mimics the visual signature of an approaching predator, allowing scientists to isolate the precise moment when the nervous system translates that signal into a motor response. By quantifying the threshold, researchers can now model how changes in water clarity, ambient light, or background motion might shift the escape trigger, potentially altering survival rates in a changing ocean.

Understanding these thresholds is also valuable for reef management. Artificial reef structures, diver‑operated deterrents, or even low‑tech devices that emit looming visual cues could be employed to steer fish away from hazardous areas such as fishing nets or polluted zones. Conversely, the data warns that any human‑generated disturbances that inadvertently exceed the escape threshold – for example, fast‑moving underwater drones or sudden light flashes – could cause chronic stress or displacement of sensitive species.

Looking ahead, the research team plans to expand the study to other reef systems and to test whether different species possess distinct looming thresholds. They also aim to integrate acoustic cues, as many predators combine visual and sound signals during hunts. By building a more comprehensive picture of how reef fish assess risk, scientists hope to develop targeted interventions that protect biodiversity while maintaining the delicate balance of predator‑prey interactions that underpin healthy coral ecosystems.
